title: Yellow Fever Trends, Seasonality and Cluster in Guinea Following DHIS Implementation (2019-2023): Implications for Pandemic Preparedness
content: Understanding the epidemiology of common causes of fever is important for effective case management, infectious disease control and for pandemic preparedness. Yellow fever (YF), a mosquito-borne viral disease endemic in Guinea, represents one such cause of AFI and remains a priority epidemic-prone disease. We analysed routine YF surveillance data from Guinea's national DHIS2 platform between 2019 and 2023 to describe temporal trends and seasonality. National and subnational notification data were examined using time-series methods, including linear and negative binomial regression, supplemented by multilevel modelling across administrative regions. During the study period, 712 suspected YF cases were reported. The median age was 17 years and 59% of cases were male. Suspected cases were reported from all administrative regions, with the highest numbers recorded in Labé and Faranah. Two notable clusters were identified: one in Labé in November 2020 and one in Faranah in December 2022, corresponding to recognised outbreak events. No significant seasonal variation was observed at national or subnational level, and no significant temporal trend in notifications was identified. These findings suggest continued endemic transmission without evidence of sustained increase or decline during the study period. The ability of routine surveillance systems to detect recognised outbreaks indicates that recent investments in surveillance infrastructure have strengthened monitoring capacity. More broadly, the findings highlight how endemic febrile illnesses such as YF form part of the epidemiological background against which emerging pathogens must be detected, reinforcing the close relationship between routine infectious disease control and pandemic preparedness.
